A circular iceberg is melting in such a way that the superficial circle is decreasing its area at a rate of $24\pi \,{\text{km}}^{2}\text{/year}.$ Calculate the rate at which the circumference of the iceberg is decreasing at the moment when the radius is  $6\,\text{km}.$

A small, circular ink blot spreads on a paper. If the blot’s circumference is increasing at a rate of $4\pi \,\text{mm}/\text{s}$, calculate the rate of change of its area at the moment when the radius is $10\,\text{mm}.$ Do not round the answer.

The area of the ink blot is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}} ${\text{mm}}^{2}/\text{s}.$
feedback.worked_solution:
In this situation, we want to find $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}$ at the moment when $r=10,$ and we are also told that  $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}=4\pi .$

To start, let's set up an equation relating the area $A$ and the circumference $C$ of the circle. Since $C=2\pi r$ and $A=\pi {r}^{2},$ the relationship between $A$ and $C$ is

$$
A=\pi {r}^{2}=\pi {(\frac{C}{2\pi })}^{2}=\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }.
$$

Differentiating this relationship with respect to $t$ using implicit differentiation, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(A) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}C}(\frac{{C}^{2}}{4\pi }) \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}\cdot \frac{C}{2\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

When $r=10\,\text{mm},$ $C=2\pi (10)=20\pi \text{ mm}.$ Hence, substituting $\frac{\text{d}C}{\text{d}t}=4\pi $ and $C=20\pi $, and solving for $\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =4\pi \cdot \frac{20\pi }{2\pi } \\ \frac{\text{d}A}{\text{d}t} & =40\pi .\end{aligned}
$$

We conclude that the area is increasing at a rate of $40\pi {\text{ mm}}^{2}\text{/s}.$
